a: Once these agreements were concluded
p: The peace of chapter 11 did not hold. Local commanders went on attacking the Jews.
b: Chapter 11 ended with letters of Lysias and the king that ended the decrees against the Jews (11:16–38). The writer now shows that peace at the top meant little on the ground: the regional governors, and the Greek cities of the coast and of Gilead, went on harassing Jewish communities. The campaigns that follow (12:3–31) match those of 1 Maccabees 5, where Judas and Simon rescue Jews in Galilee and Gilead. 1 Maccabees puts them in 164/163 BC, after the rededication and before the death of Antiochus IV is reported; 2 Maccabees puts them after the treaties. The two books order the events differently, and historians usually prefer the order of 1 Maccabees.

a: Nicanor the Cypriarch
p: A Cypriarch was the governor of Cyprus. Whether he is the Nicanor of chapters 14–15 is uncertain.
b: Kypriarchēs was the title of the governor of Cyprus under the Ptolemies of Egypt, and the island was briefly in Seleucid hands under Antiochus IV. This Nicanor may have held that post and kept the title, or he led Cypriot mercenaries. Nicanor was a common Macedonian name. The Nicanor sent by Demetrius I in chapter 14 had been "master of the elephants" (14:12), and the earlier Nicanor son of Patroclus led the army of chapter 8. Whether any two of these are one man is uncertain.

a: The people of Joppa carried out an impious deed this great
p: Joppa was a Greek port city with a Jewish minority. Its citizens drowned the Jews under cover of friendship.
b: Joppa (Jaffa) was the main port of Judea, but in the 160s BC it was a Greek city with its own council and assembly, and Jews lived there as a minority. The phrase "the city's common decree" (12:4) suggests the city voted for the boat outing and the Jews agreed as fellow residents. The story belongs to a pattern the book stresses: Greek neighbors turn on Jews when royal power weakens. Joppa became Jewish only under Jonathan and Simon, who took it and settled it with Jews (1 Maccabees 12:33–34; 13:11; 14:5).

a: called on God the just Judge
p: The title frames the chapter: God judges the killers at Joppa, and later the dead at Adullam (12:41).
b: Judas calls on "God the just Judge" before he punishes Joppa, and the men at Adullam bless "the just Judge" when the hidden sin of the dead comes to light (12:41). The idea is old: "the Judge of all the earth" does right (Genesis 18:25), and the psalmist says, "God is a judge who does right" (Psalm 7:11). In 2 Maccabees the title carries the book's theology of retribution: God repays the guilty in kind, whether Gentile or Jew. The same God who avenges Joppa's victims also lets the guilty soldiers fall.

a: two hundred forty stadia off
p: Jamnia is about 45 kilometers from Jerusalem, over the hills. The glow seen from Jerusalem is a writer's flourish.
b: A stadium was about 185 meters, so 240 stadia is about 44 kilometers, close to the real distance from Jerusalem to Jamnia (Yavneh) and its harbor. But the Judean hills stand between them, and a harbor fire would hardly have been visible from the city. The writer means that news of the burning reached Jerusalem as though one could see it. Historians often note how 2 Maccabees uses such vivid touches, after the style of Hellenistic "tragic" history, to make readers feel the events.

a: Arabs attacked him
p: Nomad Arabs attack, then make terms with Judas. 1 Maccabees 5:25 has friendly Nabateans instead.
b: The "Arabs" are called "nomads" in 12:11. In 1 Maccabees the Nabateans, Arab traders of the region east and south of the Dead Sea, meet Judas in peace and tell him of the Jews shut up in Gilead (1 Maccabees 5:24–25). 2 Maccabees has a battle first and then a treaty, with the nomads promising livestock and help. Both books show that Judas was willing to make terms with peoples who were not his enemies. Later the Nabatean kings were allies and rivals of the Hasmoneans by turns.

a: Its name was Caspin
p: Caspin is probably the Chaspho of 1 Maccabees 5:26, 36, east of the Sea of Galilee.
b: 1 Maccabees lists Chaspho among the towns of Gilead where Jews were shut in, and says Judas took it (1 Maccabees 5:26, 36). Caspin is likely the same town, perhaps modern Khisfin in the Golan. The Greek says Judas "bridged" (gephyroun) toward it, apparently building a causeway or ramp; Venetus leaves out the word. The Latin turns it into a feature of the city: "strong with bridges and walls". The "lake" of 12:16 may be a pool beside the town or the Sea of Galilee itself.

a: who brought Jericho crashing down in Joshua's day
p: Judas's men pray to the God of Joshua, who took Jericho without siege engines.
b: The men of Caspin trust their walls (12:14), so Judas's men call on the God who threw down Jericho "without rams or machines of war". Joshua tells how "the wall collapsed where it stood" (Joshua 6:20) at the shout of the people. 2 Maccabees often reminds readers of earlier deliverances in prayers before battle: Sennacherib's army (8:19; 15:22) and Jericho here. The point is that victory comes from God, not from siege craft; but the next verse has the men storming the wall "like wild beasts".

a: made a slaughter beyond words
p: The chapter counts tens of thousands of enemy dead. Readers have long been troubled by its tone.
b: Chapter 12 reports 10,000 killed at a stronghold (12:19), 30,000 in a rout (12:23), 25,000 at Carnion (12:26) and 25,000 at Ephron (12:28), with a lake that seemed full of blood (12:16). The numbers are not historical counts; ancient writers used round, huge figures for victories. The writer tells these as just punishment of cities that had harmed Jews, and also shows restraint where it was deserved: Scythopolis is spared because it had treated Jews well (12:29–31). Jewish and Christian readers have differed over such passages: some read them as the language of holy war that belongs to its time, others as models of courage. The book itself does not linger on the dead but on the prayers.

a: Tubians
p: The Jews of the land of Tob, east of the Jordan, home of the Tobiad family.
b: 1 Maccabees 5:13 reports that the Jews "in the district of Tobias" had been killed and their families taken captive. The region, in northern Transjordan, is probably the land of Tob, where Jephthah settled (Judges 11:3). The region was also linked with the powerful Tobiad family, whose seat at Araq el-Emir in Transjordan still stands. Josephus tells how the Tobiads served both Ptolemies and Seleucids (Antiquities 12.154–236). These "Tubians" were Jews of that region.

a: Dositheus and Sosipater, officers of Maccabeus
p: Two of Judas's officers have Greek names. The revolt did not reject everything Greek.
b: Dositheus ("God's gift") and Sosipater ("savior of his father") are Greek names, and Jews of the time often bore them, sometimes beside Hebrew ones. Dositheus is a translation of Hebrew names like Nathanael or Mattaniah. That Judas's officers had such names shows that the struggle was not against Greek language or names as such, but against the forced abandonment of the law (6:1–11). The book itself is written in polished Greek for Greek-speaking Jews.

a: Carnion
p: Carnion is Carnaim, where 1 Maccabees says Judas burned a temple with those who fled into it.
b: Carnion is Carnaim, an old town in Bashan, known in Genesis 14:5 as Ashteroth-karnaim, "Astarte of the two horns". 1 Maccabees says the enemy fled "to the sacred precinct at Carnaim" and Judas's men "burned the precinct with fire, with everyone in it" (1 Maccabees 5:43–44). 2 Maccabees calls the shrine an Atargateion (12:26), a temple of the Syrian goddess Atargatis. The place was "hard to besiege", but it fell.

a: from the appearance of the one who sees all things
p: Epiphaneia, God's showing of himself to help, is the book's signature word. It returns at 14:15 and 15:34.
b: Epiphaneia is the Greek for the sudden showing of a god's power, a word the Greeks used of gods who helped their cities and kings used as a title (Antiochus IV "Epiphanes"). 2 Maccabees turns it against him: the true God "appears" to defend his people (2:21; 3:24; 5:4; 14:15; 15:27 in Venetus). Here no figure is seen; the enemy feels fear "from the appearance of the one who sees all things" and panics. Swete's text spells it epiphanias.

a: the shrine of Atargatis
p: Atargatis was the great goddess of Syria, worshiped at Hierapolis and Ashkelon.
b: Atargatis, also called Derketo, was the chief goddess of northern Syria, with her great temple at Hierapolis-Bambyce and a famous shrine at Ashkelon, where she was shown as half woman, half fish. The Greek writer Lucian described her cult in The Syrian Goddess (second century AD). At Carnaim she seems to have taken over the old shrine of Astarte. 2 Maccabees treats the shrine only as a place of refuge for Judas's enemies.

a: Ephron
p: A walled town that blocked the road; 1 Maccabees 5:46–51 tells the same story.
b: In 1 Maccabees, Ephron "guarded the way in" (1 Maccabees 5:46): the road to Judea ran through it, and when its people refused passage Judas took it by assault. 2 Maccabees adds the young defenders on the walls and the stores of siege machines and missiles, to make the victory look greater. The site is usually placed near modern Irbid, in northern Jordan. On the KJV's Lysias, see the variant.

a: the Jews settled there spoke up for the people of Scythopolis
p: The Jews of Beth-shan vouched for their Greek neighbors, and Judas spared the city.
b: Scythopolis was the Greek name of Beth-shan, at the meeting of the Jordan and Jezreel valleys. 1 Maccabees mentions only that Judas crossed "into the great plain facing Beth-shan" (1 Maccabees 5:52). 2 Maccabees adds that its Jewish residents spoke for the Gentile citizens, who had treated them kindly, and Judas thanked them. Set against Joppa and Jamnia (12:3–9), the story shows the writer's rule: good will toward the Jews is repaid with good will.

a: the Feast of Weeks
p: The feast of Weeks came fifty days after Passover, so Greek speakers called it Pentecost, "fiftieth".
b: The Torah counts seven weeks from the first sheaf to the Feast of Weeks (Leviticus 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 16:9–10). Greek-speaking Jews called it Pentēkostē, "the fiftieth (day)", the name used here and in Tobit 2:1 and Acts 2:1. Judas brings his army home in time for one of the three pilgrim feasts, as a pious leader should. The holiday also dates the campaign: the spring and early summer of 163 BC.
orig: ἡ τῶν ἑβδομάδων ἑορτή ... πεντηκοστή (hē tōn hebdomadōn heortē ... pentēkostē)

a: Gorgias, governor of Idumea
p: Gorgias had fought Judas before. 1 Maccabees 5:55–62 tells of his victory over two of Judas's officers.
b: Gorgias was one of the generals sent against Judas in 165 BC (8:9; 1 Maccabees 3:38; 4:1–25). In 1 Maccabees he defeats Joseph and Azariah, who had attacked Jamnia against orders (1 Maccabees 5:55–62). Here he is governor of Idumea, the land south of Judea, and the battle goes better for the Jews, though "a few" fall (12:34). It is these few whose bodies Judas recovers at 12:39.

a: Gorgias got away to Marisa
p: Marisa was the chief city of Idumea. Its painted tombs of the 200s BC survive.
b: Marisa (Maresha) lay in the foothills southwest of Jerusalem. In the Hellenistic period it was a mixed city of Idumeans, Phoenicians and Greeks, and its painted burial caves, with Greek inscriptions and animal friezes, have been excavated. John Hyrcanus took it some time after 129 BC and made its people accept circumcision (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254–257, who gives no year; the excavators date its fall to about 112–108 BC). The Thracian horseman who saves Gorgias was one of the mercenaries Seleucid armies used.

a: in his fathers' tongue
p: Judas raises the war shout and hymns in Hebrew or Aramaic, not in Greek.
b: "The ancestral voice" (hē patrios phōnē) is the book's phrase for the Jews' own language, used by the mother and her sons (7:8, 21, 27) and by the army after the victory over Nicanor (15:29). It probably means Hebrew, the language of prayer and of holy war, though Aramaic was the daily speech of Judea. A Greek-speaking reader in Egypt would feel the contrast: at the moment of battle, Judas speaks the language of Israel's fathers.

a: they made themselves clean according to custom
p: The soldiers had touched the dead, so they purified themselves before the Sabbath.
b: The law required anyone who had killed or touched a dead body in war to purify himself on the third and seventh days (Numbers 31:19, 24). Judas's men do so "according to custom" and keep the Sabbath at Adullam, the old town where David once hid (1 Samuel 22:1). The book takes care to show its heroes keeping the law even in war: they stopped the pursuit on the Sabbath earlier (8:25–28). This care for purity frames what comes next: some of the dead had broken the law.

a: to restore them, with their kin, to their family tombs
p: Judas's men bring the dead home to family tombs, the oldest Israelite hope for a good burial.
b: To be laid with one's fathers was the proper end of a life (Genesis 49:29; 2 Samuel 21:14). Families in Judea used rock-cut tombs where bones were gathered over generations, and the dead of a battle were brought home if possible. The delay of a day, forced by the Sabbath, is noted because burial was normally done quickly. The contrast is with the wicked in this book, who die far from home and unburied (5:10; 9:28; 13:7).

a: objects consecrated to the idols of Jamnia
p: The Greek hierōmata are sacred objects, probably small amulets or charms of the gods of Jamnia.
b: Hierōmata means "consecrated things". Worn under the tunic, they were most likely amulets or tokens taken as loot at Jamnia (12:8–9) and kept for protection in battle. Soldiers of every army carried such charms. The writer does not say the men worshiped the gods of Jamnia; they had kept things the law told Israel to burn (Deuteronomy 7:25–26). That is enough for him to explain why these men, and only these, had died.

a: things the law keeps the Jews away from
p: Deuteronomy forbids keeping the silver and gold of idols, "or it will be a trap for you".
b: Deuteronomy commands Israel to burn the images of the nations' gods and adds: "Do not bring anything abhorrent into your house, or you will be put under the ban as it is" (Deuteronomy 7:26). The story at Adullam recalls Achan, who kept banned plunder from Jericho, so that Israel fell before its enemies at Ai until the sin was found and punished (Joshua 7:11–12, 21). Here, too, a hidden sin explains a defeat. Unlike Achan, these men are already dead, and the living ask God to forgive them.

a: the just Judge who brings hidden things into the open
p: God makes the hidden sin plain, as in the story of Achan.
b: The army blesses God for showing them the cause of the deaths. The phrase recalls the conviction that God sees what is hidden (Psalm 90:8; Daniel 2:22) and will bring it to light (Ecclesiastes 12:14). In Joshua 7 the hidden sin was found by lot; here it is found when the bodies are prepared for burial. The writer counts it as God's justice that only the guilty died, which makes the next step, prayer for those same men, all the more striking.

a: They asked that the sin that had been done be wiped away entirely
p: The prayer asks God to blot the sin out completely. It is a prayer for the dead men, not only for the living.
b: Exaleiphthēnai is the Septuagint's word for blotting out sin, as in "wipe out my rebellions" (Psalm 51:1). The soldiers ask that the sin "be wiped away entirely". Since the guilty men are dead, this prayer is the first sign of what verses 43–45 will explain. Some historians think the prayer and sacrifice were meant for the living army, to remove guilt from the whole camp as in Achan's case; the writer, in the verses that follow, reads them as being for the dead.

a: the noble Judas called on the people to keep clear of sin
p: Judas draws a moral for the survivors: keep yourselves free of sin. Protestant readers have stressed this.
b: Before the collection, Judas turns the event into a warning: the army has seen what sin did. Calvin, who would not argue from the book at all, held that Judas is praised only for his hope of the resurrection and that the offering itself was not free of superstition (Institutes 3.5.8). Many Protestant readers value the warning against hidden sin. Catholic interpreters answer that the warning and the prayer go together: the living are told to avoid sin and to help the dead who sinned. The verse itself sets both side by side.

a: sent it to Jerusalem to present a sacrifice for sin
t: A sin offering for the dead?
p: The law has sin offerings for the living. A sacrifice for the dead has no clear precedent in the Torah.
b: Leviticus prescribes sin offerings for sins committed unknowingly, by the priest, the community, a leader or any person (Leviticus 4). None is for the dead. Judas sends money to the temple, so the priests in Jerusalem offered the sacrifice. Whether they meant it for the army's guilt or for the dead men themselves is debated. The rabbis later read Deuteronomy 21:8, "LORD, make atonement for your people Israel, whom you ransomed" (Deuteronomy 21:8), as showing that "the dead need atonement" (Sifre on Deuteronomy 210), and Jewish custom came to give charity for the dead on Yom Kippur.

a: In doing so he did a very fine and gracious thing
p: From here to the end of 12:45 the writer explains and praises what Judas did. The comment is his.
b: Verses 43b–45 are the narrator's judgment: Judas acted "very finely and graciously" (panu kalōs kai asteiōs), with the resurrection in mind. Historians note that the writer, an epitomist working from Jason of Cyrene (2:23), adds such comments often (4:17; 5:17–20; 6:12–17). Some think Judas's own aim was to purify the living camp and the writer gave it a meaning shaped by the hope of resurrection in his own day. Catholic interpreters hold that the inspired writer's judgment is the teaching of the passage, whatever Judas himself had in mind.

a: For if he had not expected the fallen to rise again
p: If the dead do not rise, prayer for them is pointless. Paul uses a similar argument in 1 Corinthians 15:29.
b: The writer reasons backward: Judas prayed for the dead, so he expected them to rise. Resurrection is the book's great hope (7:9, 14, 23; 14:46), and Daniel 12:2 had already promised that many who sleep in the dust will awake. Paul argues in the same form about those who were "baptized for the dead": if the dead are not raised, why do it (1 Corinthians 15:29)? Both arguments assume that a practice for the dead only makes sense if death is not the end.

a: to pray for the dead
p: Kaddish and Yizkor are later Jewish prayers for the departed, though rabbinic tradition never cited this book.
b: Rabbinic Judaism does not quote 2 Maccabees, but it came to pray and give charity for the dead. The Shulchan Aruch, with the Rema's gloss, records the custom of pledging charity for the dead on Yom Kippur and mentioning their souls, "for the dead too have atonement on Yom Kippur" (Orach Chayim 621:6); this became the Yizkor service, now said on the pilgrim festivals too. Mourners say Kaddish for eleven months: the Rema explains that it is not said for twelve, since the judgment of the wicked lasts twelve months (Yoreh De'ah 376:4; compare Mishnah Eduyot 2:10). So Jewish practice also holds that the living can help the dead, without a doctrine of purgatory.

a: those who fall asleep in godliness
p: Sleep as a word for death implies waking. The writer applies it to the godly dead.
b: Koimōmenois, "those falling asleep", is an old way of speaking of death, but in a book about resurrection it carries hope: sleepers wake (Daniel 12:2). Paul and early Christians used the same verb of believers who had died (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15). The phrase raises a question the passage leaves open: the men had died in sin, yet the writer counts them among those who "fall asleep in godliness". Catholic readers see here the case of the faithful who die with sins still to be cleansed; others think the writer simply assumed they were faithful Jews who had erred.
orig: τοῖς μετ᾽ εὐσεβίας κοιμωμένοις (tois met' eusebias koimōmenois)

a: That is why he had atonement made for the dead, to free them from the sin
t: Purgatory and prayer for the dead
p: The key text for prayer for the dead. Churches draw different conclusions; see the card below.
b: "He made the atonement for the dead" (peri tōn tethnēkotōn ton exilasmon epoiēsato), "to be released from the sin". The Catholic Church cites the verse for prayer and sacrifice for the dead and for purification after death (Catechism 1032). The Orthodox pray for the dead and use the passage, but reject the Latin teaching of a purgatorial fire. Lutheran and Reformed churches reject the book's authority for doctrine and do not pray for the dead in the Catholic sense; Anglican teaching rejects "the Romish doctrine concerning Purgatory" (Article XXII). The question is carded in chapter 12 below, with each church's own words.
orig: τὸν ἐξιλασμὸν ἐποιήσατο, τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἀπολυθῆναι (ton exilasmon epoiēsato, tēs hamartias apolythēnai)

a: In the year 149
p: The Seleucid year 149 ran from autumn 164 to autumn 163 BC. 1 Maccabees 6:20 dates the siege to the year 150.
b: 2 Maccabees dates the invasion of Antiochus V to the year 149 of the Seleucid era, about 163 BC; 1 Maccabees dates the siege of the Citadel and the king's response to the year 150 (1 Maccabees 6:20). The two books may be counting from different starting points, autumn or spring, a difference that would explain several of their dates. Antiochus V Eupator was a boy of about ten; Lysias ruled in his name as "guardian" (13:2). The writer gives 2 Maccabees 13 only one invasion; 1 Maccabees 6 tells the same campaign at length.

a: twenty-two elephants and three hundred scythed chariots
p: 1 Maccabees 6:30 has thirty-two elephants. Scythed chariots appear only here.
b: Elephants were the Seleucids' pride. The Treaty of Apamea (188 BC) had ordered them to give up their elephants, but Antiochus IV paraded dozens at Daphne in 166 BC (Polybius 30.25), and Rome sent envoys to hamstring them in 162 BC. 1 Maccabees counts thirty-two elephants and describes their towers and drivers (1 Maccabees 6:30, 34–37). Chariots with scythes on their wheels were an old Persian weapon, used by Antiochus III at Magnesia. The army figures, 110,000 foot and 5,300 horse, are inflated, as in 1 Maccabees 6:30.

a: Menelaus threw in his lot with them too
p: Menelaus bought the high priesthood in 172 BC. His death here closes the story of the Hellenizing high priests.
b: Menelaus outbid Jason for the high priesthood (4:23–25), was not of the high-priestly family (the book calls his brother Simon a Benjaminite at 3:4 and 4:23), had Onias murdered (4:34), and guided Antiochus IV in robbing the temple (5:15). Josephus says he was put to death after ten years as high priest, on Lysias's advice that he was "the origin of all the mischief" (Antiquities 12.384–385). 1 Maccabees never names him. Here he hopes the boy king will confirm him in office, but the king of kings has other plans.

a: the King of kings
p: A title of Persian kings, given here to God, who turns the young king's anger against Menelaus.
b: Persian kings called themselves "king of kings", as in "Artaxerxes, king of kings" (Ezra 7:12; compare Daniel 2:37). Jewish writers gave the title to God, who rules every king: here it is God who "woke" the king's fury. The New Testament uses it of Christ: "he is Lord of lords and King of kings" (Revelation 17:14; compare 1 Timothy 6:15). The writer's point is irony: Menelaus came to court the earthly king and was destroyed by the heavenly one.

a: Lysias pointed him out as the cause of every evil
p: Josephus also says Lysias blamed Menelaus and had him killed at Beroea, and that Alcimus followed him.
b: Josephus tells that Lysias advised the king to kill Menelaus, since he had persuaded Antiochus IV to force the Jews from their ancestral worship and so caused all the trouble; the king sent him to Beroea and had him put to death there, after ten years as high priest, and gave the office to Alcimus (Antiquities 12.384–386). Beroea is Aleppo in northern Syria. The Seleucid court was making peace with the Jews (11:22–26), and Menelaus was a useful scapegoat.

a: There is a tower in that place fifty cubits high, full of ashes
p: A Persian punishment: the condemned was dropped into a tower of hot ash and smothered.
b: A tower of about 23 meters held a bed of ash, with a turning device that tipped the victim in. Greek writers on Persia describe this as a Persian penalty for the worst crimes: Ctesias tells of nobles killed in ashes under Darius II, and Valerius Maximus (9.2, external 6) describes a walled space filled with ash into which the condemned were thrown. The Seleucids inherited the old Persian lands and some of their customs. The writer needs no comment: the punishment fits the crime (13:8).

a: without even being given earth for a grave
p: Menelaus is not buried, like Jason before him. The book counts this the worst end.
b: Burial was a sacred duty, and to be left unburied was a curse (Jeremiah 22:19; Psalm 79:3). 2 Maccabees gives this end to the book's villains: Jason, who left others unburied, "received no burial of any kind" (5:10); Antiochus IV died in a strange land (9:28). Menelaus, smothered in ash, does not even get "earth". The contrast is with the faithful dead of Adullam, carried home to family tombs (12:39), and with Razis, who dies hoping to receive his body back (14:46).

a: He had sinned much around the altar, whose fire was pure, and its ash too
p: Menelaus defiled the altar, whose fire and ash were holy, so he died in ash.
b: The law kept the altar fire burning: "Fire is to keep burning on the altar without a break" (Leviticus 6:13), and its ashes were carried to a clean place (Leviticus 6:10–11). Menelaus, as high priest, had served at that altar while selling its vessels (4:32, 39) and leading the king into the sanctuary (5:15). He dies by the matching element. This is the book's favorite pattern of justice: Andronicus is killed where he killed Onias (4:38), Jason dies unburied (5:10), Antiochus is struck in the bowels (9:5–6), and Nicanor loses the hand he raised against the temple (15:30–32).

a: pleading with the merciful Lord through weeping and fasting and lying on the ground for three days on end
p: The people fast for three days, the same length as Esther's fast before she went to the king.
b: Fasting, weeping and lying on the ground were the signs of a people in mourning and in need (Joel 2:12; Nehemiah 9:1). Three days is the length of Esther's fast: "For three days, night and day, eat nothing and drink nothing" (Esther 4:16). In 2 Maccabees every major battle is preceded by such prayer (8:2–4; 10:25–26; 15:21–24). The writer wants the reader to see that victory follows repentance and pleading.

a: He passed the password "God's victory" to those around him
p: Armies used passwords to recognize their own in the dark. Judas's are always confessions of faith.
b: Greek armies chose a synthēma, a password, before battle, especially for night attacks, and it was often a god's name: Xenophon's army once used "Zeus Savior, Victory". Judas's passwords are "God's help" (8:23) and "God's victory" here, so the very word that keeps the men together in the dark confesses who wins. The night raid recalls Gideon (Judges 7:19–22).

a: he laid low the chief of the elephants, together with the man in its housing
p: 2 Maccabees has Judas kill the lead elephant. 1 Maccabees tells of Eleazar dying under one.
b: In 1 Maccabees, Judas's brother Eleazar sees a royal elephant, runs under it and kills it, and dies when it falls on him (1 Maccabees 6:43–46). 2 Maccabees, which never mentions that battle at Beth-zechariah or Judas's retreat, gives Judas a night raid that strikes down the leading elephant and the man in its "house", the tower on its back. The two accounts may grow from the same memory. 1 Maccabees admits that Judas withdrew to Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 6:47); 2 Maccabees tells only of success.

a: He came at Beth-zur
p: In 1 Maccabees 6:49 Beth-zur surrenders for lack of food in a Sabbath year. Here it holds out.
b: Beth-zur, south of Jerusalem on the road to Hebron, was the fortress Judas had built up after the rededication (1 Maccabees 4:61). 1 Maccabees says the king made peace with its people and they came out, "because they had no food there to last a siege, for it was a Sabbath year for the land" (1 Maccabees 6:49). 2 Maccabees has a string of failed royal assaults, supplies sent in by Judas, a traitor caught (13:21), and then an agreement (13:22). Both books end in terms, but 2 Maccabees leaves out the defeat.

a: had rebelled in desperation
p: The Greek means Philip had gone mad, or acted in desperation: he had rebelled at Antioch.
b: Aponenoēsthai is used of desperate, reckless acts, here of open revolt. Philip, a Friend of Antiochus IV, had been named guardian of the young king when Antiochus died (1 Maccabees 6:14–15, 55–56), so Lysias's rule was challenged. 2 Maccabees earlier says Philip fled to Egypt with the king's body (9:29). The news forced Lysias to make peace and hurry back. The KJV renders "was desperately bent".

a: He paid honor to the temple and the place, and showed kindness
p: 2 Maccabees has the king honor the temple. 1 Maccabees says he broke his oath and tore down its wall.
b: The two books agree that Lysias and the king made peace in haste because of Philip, but they remember the peace differently. 2 Maccabees stresses the honors: an oath, a sacrifice, gifts for the temple and favor for Judas (13:23–24). 1 Maccabees says the king "broke the oath he had sworn, and gave orders to tear down the wall all around" Mount Zion (1 Maccabees 6:62). 2 Maccabees likes to show foreign kings honoring the temple (3:2–3; 9:16), as proof that the God of the temple is greater than they are.

a: Lysias stepped up to the platform
p: Lysias explains the treaty to the people of Ptolemais from the speaker's platform, in Greek civic style.
b: The bēma was the speaker's platform in a Greek city's assembly. Ptolemais (Acco) was a Greek city, hostile to the Jews (1 Maccabees 5:15, 22), and its citizens resented a treaty that protected them. Even the regent had to argue his case before them. The scene shows the limits of royal power in the Hellenistic cities, and the short, clipped verbs of 13:22–26 ("He persuaded them, softened them, put them in a good humor") mimic the speed of events.

a: Demetrius son of Seleucus had put in at the port of Tripolis
p: Demetrius, a hostage in Rome, escaped in 162 BC and seized the throne from his young cousin.
b: Demetrius I was the son of Seleucus IV and the rightful heir; he had been held in Rome as a hostage. When Antiochus IV died, the Senate kept him there, and he escaped by ship in 162 BC with the help of friends, including the historian Polybius (Polybius 31.11–15). He landed at Tripolis on the Phoenician coast, and the army went over to him. "In the year 151 Demetrius son of Seleucus left Rome" (1 Maccabees 7:1). The "three years" are counted from the rededication or from the events of chapter 11.

a: had killed Antiochus and his guardian Lysias
p: 1 Maccabees 7:2–4 says the army seized the boy king and Lysias, and Demetrius had them killed.
b: 2 Maccabees gives the change of rulers in a few words. 1 Maccabees adds that the troops seized Antiochus V and Lysias to hand them over, and that Demetrius said, "Do not show me their faces", and the soldiers killed them (1 Maccabees 7:2–4). Antiochus V was about eleven. The writer, who opened chapter 13 with the boy king's invasion, closes his reign without comment.

a: There was one Alcimus, high priest before
p: Alcimus (Yakim) was a priest of Aaron's line. 1 Maccabees 7 and Josephus tell his story differently.
b: Alcimus is Greek for the Hebrew name Yakim or Eliakim. 1 Maccabees calls him one "who wanted to serve as priest" (1 Maccabees 7:5), and the Hasideans trusted him as "a priest of the line of Aaron" (1 Maccabees 7:14). Josephus says Antiochus V had already made him high priest after Menelaus (Antiquities 12.385), which agrees with "high priest before" here. 2 Maccabees adds that he had defiled himself of his own free will during the persecution, and so could not hope to serve at the altar again.

a: a golden crown and a palm, and some of the temple's customary branches as well
p: A golden crown was the usual gift to a new king. The palm and the temple's branches add victory and honor.
b: Cities and envoys gave Hellenistic kings golden crowns on their accession, and the crown tax that grew out of the custom appears in the letters of 1 Maccabees (1 Maccabees 10:29; 13:39). The palm branch was a sign of victory. Tois nomizomenois thallōn tou hierou means the branches customary at the temple, perhaps those carried at its festivals, as at the Feast of Booths and the rededication (10:7). Alcimus, who could no longer serve at the altar (14:3), brings the temple's own tokens to win the king. He said nothing that day and waited for the right moment.
orig: τοῖς νομιζομένοις θαλλῶν τοῦ ἱεροῦ (tois nomizomenois thallōn tou hierou)

a: The Jews they call Hasideans, led by Judas Maccabeus
p: Alcimus calls Judas the Hasideans' leader. In 1 Maccabees 7:13 the Hasideans first trust Alcimus.
b: The Hasideans (Hasidim, "loyal ones") joined Mattathias early (1 Maccabees 2:42). In 1 Maccabees they seek peace from Alcimus as a priest of Aaron's line, and he kills sixty of them in one day (1 Maccabees 7:13–16). Here Alcimus tells the king that Judas leads them. Historians have long debated whether the Hasideans were a distinct party, perhaps the forerunners of the Pharisees or the Essenes, or simply the devout who supported the revolt. 2 Maccabees seems to treat Judas's followers and the Hasideans as one.

a: the other Friends
p: "Friends" was a court rank. The Friends were the king's council and senior officers.
b: In Hellenistic kingdoms the philoi, "Friends", were the king's inner circle, ranked in grades ("First Friends" in 1 Maccabees 10:65). They held commands and governed provinces. Alcimus counts himself among them, and "the other Friends" share his dislike of Judas. Nicanor, whom Demetrius sends next, was one of them. The site writes the title with a capital to show it is a rank.

a: Nicanor, once master of the elephants
p: Nicanor commanded the royal elephants. 1 Maccabees calls him "a man who hated Israel".
b: 1 Maccabees introduces him as "one of his honored commanders, a man who hated Israel and was its enemy" (1 Maccabees 7:26). Josephus says he was among those who fled Rome with Demetrius (Antiquities 12.402). Whether he is the same Nicanor who led the army of 165 BC (8:9–36) is uncertain; the writer does not link them. In 2 Maccabees he will be first Judas's friend, then the temple's enemy, and his day of defeat the book's last feast.

a: the greatest temple
p: The royal letter calls Jerusalem's temple "the greatest". It is the Greek of royal courtesy.
b: Tou megistou hierou, "of the greatest temple", is the kind of phrase royal letters used for honored sanctuaries, and the book's narrator also calls the temple "great and holy" (14:31). Coming from a king who orders Judas's arrest, it shows the double attitude of the Seleucid court: honor for the temple, war on its defenders. Venetus has "the great temple".

a: the Jews threw earth over themselves
p: Throwing earth or dust on the head was a rite of mourning and pleading.
b: Joshua and the elders "threw dust on their heads" after the defeat at Ai (Joshua 7:6), and the people of Nehemiah's time fasted "with soil on them" (Nehemiah 9:1). The Jews do the same at the news of Nicanor's coming. The prayer that follows calls God the one who "set up his people to last for all time", recalling the covenant, and who helps "his own portion", the old name for Israel as God's share (Deuteronomy 32:9).

a: he was wary of having the issue decided in blood
p: In 2 Maccabees Nicanor seeks peace in earnest. In 1 Maccabees his peace was a trick from the start.
b: The two books differ sharply here. 1 Maccabees says Nicanor "sent a treacherous message of peace" and "the enemy were ready to seize Judas" (1 Maccabees 7:27–29). 2 Maccabees tells of a real treaty, private talks with guards posted (14:21–22), and a friendship that lasts until Alcimus stirs up the king. Many historians think 2 Maccabees keeps a more accurate memory and 1 Maccabees blackened Nicanor from the start. Others think 2 Maccabees builds the friendship so that Nicanor's later turn against the temple looks all the worse.

a: He pressed him to take a wife and raise a family
p: For a short time Judas lives a settled life, married and in public affairs, under Nicanor's protection.
b: This picture of Judas as a married man taking part in everyday life is found nowhere else. 1 Maccabees mentions no wife or children of Judas. The writer may draw on Jason of Cyrene's fuller account, or he may use the scene to set up the coming reversal: Judas, who had wanted peace, is driven back into hiding by royal orders (14:27–30). The phrase "took his part in everyday life" may also mean he shared in public office.

a: appointed Judas, who schemed against his kingdom, as successor
p: A diadochos was a successor or deputy. The witnesses differ on whose successor Alcimus says Judas was made.
b: Diadochos means successor, and in Hellenistic courts it was also a rank, a deputy who could take over a command. In Alexandrinus, Alcimus says Nicanor had appointed "the plotter against his kingdom", meaning the king's, as successor, apparently to Nicanor's own command. Venetus moves the pronoun: Judas is made "his successor". The KJV says "to be the king's successor", which would be a charge of treason against the throne itself. Whether true or slander, the king believes it. Alcimus, who had lost his place at the altar (14:3), had most to lose from a peace with Judas. See the variant.
orig: τὸν γὰρ ἐπίβουλον τῆς βασιλείας αὐτοῦ Ἰούδαν διάδοχον ἀπέδειξεν (ton gar epiboulon tēs basileias autou Ioudan diadochon apedeixen)

a: I will put up a temple to Dionysus for all to see
p: Nicanor threatens to replace the temple with one to Dionysus, a god the persecution had already forced on Jews.
b: Under Antiochus IV the Jews had been made to march in the procession of Dionysus carrying ivy (6:7). Nicanor threatens far more: to level the precinct, dig out the altar and build a temple to the god in its place. 1 Maccabees gives a different oath: "I will burn this house down" (1 Maccabees 7:35). Some scholars link Dionysus with the Greek view, found in Plutarch and Tacitus, that the Jews' God was Dionysus. The threat makes Nicanor a new Antiochus.

a: He held out his right hand toward the temple and swore
p: Nicanor swears with his right hand toward the temple. That hand will be hung up facing it.
b: Raising the right hand was the gesture of an oath. Nicanor's hand comes back three times: it is cut off with the shoulder (15:30), shown to the people as the hand he "had held out in his bragging against the holy house of the Almighty" (15:32), and hung up "facing the temple" (15:33). 1 Maccabees has the same detail: they cut off "the right hand he had stretched out so arrogantly" (1 Maccabees 7:47). The punishment matches the sin exactly.

a: The priests lifted their hands toward heaven
p: 1 Maccabees 7:36–38 also has the priests pray after Nicanor's threat, but for vengeance.
b: In 1 Maccabees the priests weep before the altar and say, "Bring vengeance on this man and on his army" (1 Maccabees 7:38). In 2 Maccabees they ask God to keep the newly cleansed house undefiled (14:36). The prayer begins with God's freedom: the Lord of all "who lack nothing" chose to dwell among his people. Both books then answer the prayer with Nicanor's death on 13 Adar.

a: who lack nothing
p: God has no need of a temple, yet chose to dwell among Israel. The paradox goes back to Solomon's prayer.
b: Aprosdeēs, "needing nothing", is a word Greek philosophers used of the divine. Solomon put the same paradox in a question: "But can God truly make his home on earth?" (1 Kings 8:27). The Psalms say God needs no sacrifices: "for the world and everything in it is mine" (Psalm 50:12). Paul tells the Athenians that God needs nothing from human hands (Acts 17:25). The priests join both truths: God lacks nothing, and was pleased to have a temple "for your dwelling among us".
orig: τῶν ὅλων ἀπροσδεὴς ὑπάρχων (tōn holōn aprosdeēs hyparchōn)

a: to have a temple for your dwelling among us
p: Skēnōsis, "tenting", recalls God's dwelling in the tabernacle. John 1:14 uses the same root.
b: Skēnōsis comes from skēnē, "tent", the word for the tabernacle in the wilderness. The priests say God was pleased to have a temple "of your tenting among us". John's Gospel uses the verb from the same root of the Word who "pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). The Hebrew idea behind both is God's dwelling (shakan, the root later used for the Shekhinah) in the midst of Israel (Exodus 25:8).
orig: ναὸν τῆς σῆς σκηνώσεως (naon tēs sēs skēnōseōs)

a: Razis, an elder of Jerusalem
p: Razis is known only from this chapter. His title, "father of the Jews", marks him as a patron of his people.
b: Nothing else is known of Razis. He is an elder of Jerusalem, "devoted to his people" (philopolitēs, "lover of his fellow citizens"), and was called "father of the Jews" for his kindness, a title like the "father of the city" given to public benefactors in Greek cities. The writer places his story between Nicanor's threat to the temple and the battle, as a second martyrdom after Eleazar and the seven brothers (6:18–7:42).

a: he had been brought to trial for Judaism
p: The word Ioudaismos first appears in 2 Maccabees, for the Jewish way of life defended against Hellenism.
b: Ioudaismos is first found in this book (2:21; 8:1; 14:38), coined on the pattern of Hellēnismos (4:13), "Greekness". It means the whole Jewish way of life, its law and loyalty, not a religion in the modern sense. Razis had "staked body and soul" on it. Paul uses the word of his own past: "when I was in Judaism" (Galatians 1:13–14). The phrase "the days of keeping apart" is the same as in 14:3; see the variant there.

a: Razis turned his sword on himself
p: The writer praises Razis. Augustine, answering the Donatists, said the deed was told, not praised.
b: The writer calls Razis's death noble (14:42–43). In North Africa the Donatist Gaudentius cited Razis to defend members of his movement who killed themselves rather than submit. Augustine answered that Scripture can narrate a deed without approving it: Razis was "not wise in choosing death" and "impatient in bearing humiliation", and his acts were "great things, but they are not good" (Letter 204, to Dulcitius; compare Against Gaudentius 1.31). Aquinas followed him: Razis acted from "a weakness of soul" (Summa II-II 64.5). Catholic teaching treats the account as narrative, not a model. Protestant critics of the book's authority often cited the praise of Razis against it.

a: He wanted a noble death
p: The writer frames Razis's death in the language of Greek and Roman honor: better death than shame.
b: Eugenōs, "nobly", and andrōdōs, "like a true man" (14:43), are words of the Greek ideal of the noble death. Greek and Roman readers admired those who chose death over capture, and Jewish history had its own cases: Saul falls on his sword so the Philistines will not abuse him (1 Samuel 31:4), and Samson dies with his enemies (Judges 16:30). Josephus argues against suicide in his own speech at Jotapata (Jewish War 3.362–382) and tells of the defenders of Masada (Jewish War 7.320–401). The writer gives Razis the honors of a martyr; whether the act was right is a separate question.

a: He called on the one who rules over life and spirit to give these back to him again
p: Razis tears out his bowels and asks God to give them back: a vivid hope for the resurrection of the body.
b: Like the third brother, who stretched out his hands saying he hoped to receive them back from God (7:11), and the mother, who trusted the Creator to give back breath and life (7:23), Razis dies asking for his very organs back. The writer believes in a bodily resurrection: not the soul escaping the body, but the same body restored. This is why the book matters to the Christian doctrine of the resurrection of the flesh, and why the details are so physical.

a: He pulled his bowels out, seized them with both hands, and flung them at the crowds
p: The grim detail belongs to the "tragic" style of Hellenistic history, which aimed to move readers.
b: Hellenistic historians often wrote to stir pity and horror, a style Polybius criticized in his rival Phylarchus (Polybius 2.56). 2 Maccabees uses it freely: the tortures of chapter 7, Antiochus's rotting body (9:9), and Razis's death here. Ancient readers would take the scene as a sign of superhuman courage. Modern readers often find it hard to bear. The writer's purpose is clear from 14:46: even in this horror, Razis looks to God for his body back.

a: he planned to fall on them on the day of rest
p: Nicanor plans to attack on the Sabbath, expecting Jews not to fight. Since 1 Maccabees 2:41 they would.
b: At the start of the revolt, a thousand Jews let themselves be killed rather than fight on the Sabbath, and Mattathias's men then decided: "Whoever comes to make war on us on the Sabbath day, we will fight him face to face" (1 Maccabees 2:41). 2 Maccabees, which stresses Sabbath-keeping (5:25–26; 8:26–28; 12:38), never mentions that decision. Here the threat ends before any battle: the Jews in Nicanor's own army protest, and his plan comes to nothing (15:5).

a: whether there was a Sovereign in heaven
p: Nicanor's mocking question echoes Pharaoh's "Who is this LORD?" (Exodus 5:2).
b: Pharaoh asked, "Who is this LORD, that I should heed his voice by letting Israel go?" (Exodus 5:2). Nicanor asks whether there is a Sovereign (dynastēs) in heaven who ordered the Sabbath, and sets himself up as "a sovereign on earth" (15:5). The word is the one the Jews use of God throughout this chapter (15:4, 23, 29). The exchange makes the battle a contest between two sovereigns, and the outcome answers the question.

a: He gave them heart from the Law and the Prophets
p: Judas encourages his men "from the Law and the Prophets", a sign of how the writer named the sacred books.
b: "The Law and the Prophets" is one of the earliest names for Israel's scriptures as a set. The grandson of Ben Sira, writing in Egypt after 132 BC, speaks of "the law, the prophets and the other books of our ancestors" (Sirach 1:0). Jesus sums up the teaching of Scripture this way: "That is the Law and the Prophets" (Matthew 7:12). The writer does not name the books he means. Earlier, Judas read aloud from the holy book before battle (8:23). The phrase tells us that by the writer's time the Law and the Prophets were the recognized heart of Scripture.

a: He told them a dream that deserved belief
p: Generals in the Greek world told of dreams before battle. Judas's is a vision of two holy men.
b: Ancient historians often report the dreams of commanders, and Greek readers expected a sign before a great battle: Alexander's dreams before Tyre are one example. Judas's dream "deserved belief" (axiopiston), the writer insists. In the Hebrew Scriptures God speaks in dreams to Joseph, Solomon and Daniel (Genesis 37:5–10; 1 Kings 3:5; Daniel 7:1). The dream gives Judas's men, outnumbered, the assurance that the holy dead and God himself stand with them.

a: Onias, the former high priest
p: Onias III, murdered about 170 BC, now prays for the nation. The book began its story with his goodness.
b: Onias III was the high priest in whose day "people lived in the holy city in complete peace" (3:1). Jason ousted him (4:7), and Menelaus had him murdered near Antioch (4:34). The description here repeats the virtues of chapter 3 in Greek ideal terms: noble and good (kalos kai agathos), modest, gentle, well spoken, trained from boyhood in virtue. Many interpreters link his murder with "an anointed one will be cut off" in Daniel 9:26. In the dream the murdered priest is alive and praying.

a: he had his hands held out and was praying for the whole Jewish community
t: The dead praying for the living
p: Onias, dead, prays for the people. This is the chief text for the intercession of departed saints.
b: The dream shows the holy dead praying for the living. Catholic theologians cite the dream for the intercession of the saints, which the Catechism teaches: those in heaven, "more closely united to Christ", do not cease to intercede (Catechism 956). The Orthodox teach the same and ask the saints' prayers in every service. The Lutheran Apology grants that the saints in heaven pray for the church in general, but denies there is warrant for invoking them (Apology XXI); Reformed and Anglican confessions reject invocation of saints (Article XXII). Revelation shows heavenly prayers as "gold bowls full of incense. These are the prayers of the saints" (Revelation 5:8). The question is carded at Revelation 5.

a: a man had appeared who stood out by his white hair and his glory
p: Jeremiah appears as a glorious old man. White hair is a sign of age, wisdom and heavenly honor.
b: White hair marks the honored elder (Proverbs 16:31; 2 Maccabees 6:23), and in Daniel's vision the Ancient of Days has hair "like pure wool" (Daniel 7:9). Jeremiah, who by tradition died in Egypt centuries before, appears in glory beside Onias. Readers of the Gospels have compared the Transfiguration, where Moses and Elijah appear with Jesus: "Suddenly the disciples saw Moses and Elijah, in conversation with him" (Matthew 17:3).

a: the one who prays much for the people and the holy city
p: In his lifetime Jeremiah was told not to pray for the people. Now he prays for them after death.
b: God told Jeremiah not to pray for the people (Jeremiah 7:16; 11:14; 14:11), and said that even Moses and Samuel could not turn him (Jeremiah 15:1). Jeremiah wept and pleaded all the same. Later tradition made him the great intercessor: 2 Maccabees itself tells how he hid the tent and ark (2:1–8), and in the Gospels some think Jesus is "Jeremiah, or one of the prophets" (Matthew 16:14). The dream continues the prophet's love for Jerusalem beyond his death. The title "lover of his brothers" (philadelphos) was also a royal epithet (Ptolemy II Philadelphus).

a: passed Judas a sword of gold
p: The prophet gives Judas a sword from God: the victory will be God's gift.
b: In the ancient Near East and in Greek tradition, a god's gift of a weapon to a king was a sign of a divine mandate. Here the gift comes through Jeremiah, the prophet who had foretold Jerusalem's fall, now arming its defender. Joshua met "the commander of the LORD's army" with a drawn sword before Jericho (Joshua 5:13–14). The sword is "holy" and "a gift from God" (15:16), and with it Judas will "smash" the enemy: the victory will not be credited to Judas's skill alone.

a: it does not depend on arms
p: Judas knows victory does not come from arms. David told Goliath the same.
b: David told Goliath that "the LORD saves, and not by sword and spear. The battle belongs to the LORD" (1 Samuel 17:47), and the psalmist said, "A king does not win safety by having a big army" (Psalm 33:16). Judas, facing elephants and cavalry, makes the same confession. 1 Maccabees puts it in Judas's mouth earlier: victory does not depend on the size of the army (1 Maccabees 3:18–19). The book adds: God gives victory "to the deserving", those whose cause is right.

a: You, Master, sent your angel when Hezekiah was king of Judea
p: Judas recalls the angel who struck the Assyrian camp, as the book did before (8:19).
b: "The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria: one hundred eighty-five thousand" (2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36). Judas cites the same deliverance before the battle against the first Nicanor (8:19), and 1 Maccabees has Judas recall it in his prayer before this same battle (1 Maccabees 7:41). The precedent fits: a blaspheming general threatens Jerusalem and its temple, and God answers the prayer of the king and the people.

a: send a good angel ahead of us
p: Judas asks for an angel to go before the army, as God promised Israel at Sinai.
b: God promised Israel: "Here, I am sending an angel in front of you to keep you safe on the way" (Exodus 23:20). Earlier the army had begged the Lord "to send a good angel" (11:6), and a rider in white appeared at their head (11:8). Tobit tells his wife, "For a good angel will go with him" (Tobit 5:22). On the readings "a good angel" and "your angel", see the variant.

a: With their hands they fought, and with their hearts they prayed to God
p: The army fights and prays at once. Readers have taken it as a model of action joined to prayer.
b: The verse balances two clauses: hands fighting, hearts praying. Christian readers made it a motto for soldiers and for the active life joined to prayer; Jewish readers would compare Moses praying on the hill while Joshua fought below (Exodus 17:11–12). The writer's theology is consistent: the men must act, but God's care gives the victory. 1 Maccabees gives the battle site, Adasa, north of Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 7:40, 45).

a: they found that Nicanor had fallen, armor and all
p: Nicanor died in the battle in March 161 BC. 1 Maccabees 7:43 says he was the first to fall.
b: 1 Maccabees says the armies met "on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar" and Nicanor "himself was the first to fall in the battle" (1 Maccabees 7:43); his army then fled. 2 Maccabees has the Jews discover his body after the fighting. Thirteen Adar of the year 151 fell in March 161 BC. Josephus also tells the battle and its yearly feast (Antiquities 12.409–412). Judas himself would die about a year later at Elasa (1 Maccabees 9:1–18), which 2 Maccabees does not tell.

a: gave orders to cut off Nicanor's head, and his hand with the shoulder, and take them to Jerusalem
p: The head of the enemy carried to Jerusalem recalls David with Goliath's head, and Judith with Holofernes'.
b: "David carried the Philistine's head to Jerusalem" (1 Samuel 17:54). Judith brings back Holofernes' head and has it hung on the wall (Judith 13:15; 14:1). In 1 Maccabees the Jews cut off Nicanor's head and right hand "and hung them up near Jerusalem" (1 Maccabees 7:47). Displaying a defeated enemy's head was common in the ancient world. The writer turns it into a lesson: the hand raised against the temple is shown before it.

a: summoned the people from the Citadel
p: The Citadel was held by a Seleucid garrison until 141 BC. The verse may compress events or mean those near it.
b: The Citadel (Akra) in Jerusalem held a royal garrison from 168 BC until Simon took it in 141 BC (1 Maccabees 13:49–51). So Judas could hardly summon people from it, or hang Nicanor's head on it (15:35). Some take the phrase to mean that Judas called the garrison to see the trophy, as a warning; others think the writer did not know the Citadel's history well, or wrote as though the later situation applied. The writer's claim that the Hebrews held the city from then on (15:37) is part of the same picture.

a: said it should be fed to the birds bit by bit
p: Alexandrinus has no verb for what is done with the tongue. Venetus adds "he would give", which the Plain supplies.
b: Alexandrinus reads "he said, bit by bit to the birds" (ephē meta meros tois orneois), with no verb. Venetus adds dōsein, "(that he) would give (it)", and the KJV has "that they should give it by pieces unto the fowls". The sense is clear, and the Plain supplies "should be fed", but the verb comes from Venetus, not from the base text.
orig: ἔφη μετὰ μέρος τοῖς ὀρνέοις (ephē meta meros tois orneois)

a: He cut out the impious Nicanor's tongue
p: The tongue that mocked God is cut out and fed to the birds. Each part is punished for its sin.
b: Nicanor blasphemed with his tongue (15:3–5, 24) and threatened the temple with his hand (14:33). So the tongue goes to the birds and the hand is hung up facing the temple. Leaving the dead to the birds was the curse of the unburied (Deuteronomy 28:26; 1 Kings 14:11). The same logic of justice ran through the deaths of Menelaus (13:8) and Antiochus (9:5–6). The writer presents it as fitting, not as cruelty.

a: the Lord who appears
p: The people bless "the Lord who appears", the book's name for the God who shows his power to help.
b: Ton epiphanē kyrion, "the manifest Lord", sums up the book's theology of God's appearances (2:21; 3:30; 12:22; 14:15). The blessing that follows, for the one "who has kept his own place free from defilement", answers the priests' prayer of 14:36 almost word for word. The book thus ends where its main story began, with the temple kept safe (3:39).

a: one day before Mordecai's Day
p: The earliest mention of Purim outside Esther, here called "Mordecai's Day" (14 Adar).
b: Esther tells how on the thirteenth day of Adar, the twelfth month, the Jews defeated those who hated them (Esther 9:1), and how they "rested on its fourteenth day and turned it into a day of feasting and joy" (Esther 9:17). 2 Maccabees calls the fourteenth "Mordecai's Day", the oldest witness to Purim outside Esther. Nicanor's Day falls on the thirteenth, the day of battle in Esther as well. The Scroll of Fasts lists "the day of Nicanor" on 13 Adar, and the Babylonian Talmud tells how his thumbs and big toes were cut off and hung at the gates of Jerusalem (Ta'anit 18b). Josephus says it was still kept in his day; it lapsed with the Scroll of Fasts, and 13 Adar is now the Fast of Esther, first attested in geonic times.

a: (in the Syrian language the month is called Adar)
p: Adar is the Babylonian month name used by Jews after the exile. It falls in February–March.
b: Jews took over the Babylonian month names during the exile; Adar appears in Esther and Ezra (Esther 3:7; Ezra 6:15). Greek writers called the shared language of the Near East, Aramaic, "Syrian". The writer explains the name for readers in Egypt who knew Macedonian month names; he also calls it "the twelfth month", the numbering of the Torah's calendar, which begins in spring.

a: From those times on the Hebrews held the city
p: The book stops at a high point. Within a year Judas was dead and Jerusalem was again under Seleucid control.
b: 1 Maccabees goes on: Demetrius sent Bacchides and Alcimus back, Judas fell at Elasa in 160 BC, and the Seleucid party held Jerusalem for years (1 Maccabees 9:1–57). 2 Maccabees ends with the temple saved and Nicanor's Day founded, as its story of the temple began with Heliodorus (chapter 3) and its middle with Hanukkah (10:1–8). The writer chose this ending: the two feasts, Hanukkah and Nicanor's Day, frame the second half of the book. "Hebrews" is the old, dignified name for the nation, used in this book for heroes (7:31; 11:13).

a: If it is thin and middling, that was all within my reach
p: The writer admits the limits of his skill. Protestant writers argued that an inspired author would not speak so.
b: The writer closes with a stock apology, as Greek historians did. Calvin argued that the writer, by asking pardon, shows his book is not an oracle of the Holy Spirit (Institutes 3.5.8), and Protestant writers repeated the point; the Latin text he read has "it must be pardoned me" (see the variant). Catholic and Orthodox writers answer that inspiration works through human authors and their effort: this writer says the summary cost "sweat and sleepless nights" (2:26), and Luke also describes his careful research (Luke 1:1–4). Vatican II calls the human writers "true authors" (Dei Verbum 11). The question is carded on the book page.

a: Wine taken on its own is bad for you, and water on its own likewise
p: Greeks drank wine mixed with water. The writer compares a well-made story to a well-mixed cup.
b: Greek custom was to mix wine with water, often one part wine to two or three of water; drinking it unmixed was thought barbarous. The writer's last image matches his first preface, which spoke of giving "enjoyment to those who want to read" (2:25) and compared his task to preparing a banquet (2:27). Isaiah uses watered wine as a picture of corruption, "your wine is watered down" (Isaiah 1:22), but here mixing is the art of pleasing a reader.

a: Here, then, will be the ending.
p: Alexandrinus ends with a title calling the book a "letter"; Venetus calls it an "epitome".
b: After the last line, Alexandrinus adds a closing title, "Of the deeds of Judas Maccabeus, a letter" (epistolē), and Venetus "an epitome" (epitomē), which is what the writer called his work (2:26, 28). "Letter" may reflect the two letters that open the book (1:1–2:18). In the KJV, which puts 2 Maccabees last among the Apocrypha, the text is followed by "The END of the APOCRYPHA".
